title: What Can We Learn From Data
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 1.1 What Can We Learn From Data
intro: Identify the population, sample, data, and investigative question, and explain why sample results do not determine population values exactly.

moments.title: Start with a study
moments.text: Collect data to answer a question about a population.

moments.title: A question with a purpose
moments.text: Choose the question before examining the results.

moments.title: Answer in context
moments.text: Name the people or items and the characteristic being studied.

moments.title: Questions determine the data
moments.text: A question about ownership requires an ownership response from each student.

moments.title: Datum and data set
moments.text: A datum describes one item; a data set collects observations.

moments.title: Population and sample
moments.text: The population is the group of interest; the sample is the subset studied.

moments.title: Statistical inference
moments.text: Use sample information to estimate or judge a population characteristic.

moments.title: Identify the study components
moments.text: Separate all college students from the students actually surveyed.

moments.title: Breakfast study
moments.text: Record breakfast information for the selected students.

moments.title: Compare race times
moments.text: Connect the drink received and the recorded race time to the question.

cards.name: Population
cards.text: Name all items or individuals the question concerns.

cards.name: Sample
cards.text: Name the subset from which data were collected.

cards.name: Investigative question
cards.text: State the population, variable, and purpose so data could answer it.

cards.name: Inference
cards.text: A sample supports an estimate, with uncertainty about the population.

questions.obj: Identify the components of a study
questions.q: David randomly selects 230 students at his large college. Of these, 141 report owning a vehicle. Identify the population, sample, data, and investigative question.

work.text: The question concerns all students at David's college.

steps.t: Identify the observed sample and data.

work.text: The sample is the 230 selected students. Each reports whether they own a vehicle.
What proportion of all students at this college own a vehicle?

questions.answer: The 141 ownership responses summarize the sample; they are not the population or the sample itself.

traps.title: Population versus respondents
traps.better: The population is all students at the college; the 230 selected students form the sample.

traps.title: A datum versus a summary
traps.better: Each student reports whether they own a vehicle; 141 is the count reporting yes.

traps.title: A question that can be answered
traps.better: Define the population and a measurable outcome, such as the proportion of students who complete a course.

traps.title: Sample certainty
traps.weak: The population must have exactly the sample percentage.
traps.better: A sample percentage estimates a population percentage and may differ from it.

questions.stem: A library asks 80 randomly selected members how many books they borrowed last month. It wants information about all current members. What is the population?
opts: The number of books per member
why: The question concerns all current members.
Books are not the group of people of interest.

questions.stem: Which question specifies collectable data and a clear population?
opts: What is the median daily travel time of students at Oak School?
why: Travel time can be measured for students at the named school.
Neither a population nor a measurable variable is specified.

questions.stem: A researcher records each sampled lamp's operating lifetime. Which is one datum?
opts: The life of one lamp: 940 hours

questions.stem: Why study a sample of parcels rather than all parcels shipped in a year?
opts: Every sample has the population mean
Measuring every parcel may be too costly
why: The full group can be defined.
Practical limits can make collecting all population data difficult.

sections.title: Write a complete response
sections.prompt: A transport office randomly selects 120 students from the current enrollment list at Pine School and records each student's travel time to school.
parts: (b) State an investigative question about mean travel time.
(c) Describe the data needed and why the sample mean may differ from the population mean.
sample: (a) The population is all currently enrolled Pine School students. The sample is the 120 selected students.
(b) What is the mean travel time to school for all currently enrolled Pine School students?

(c) Record travel time in minutes for each selected student, using a consistent definition of the journey. A different sample may contain students with different journey times, so its mean need not equal the population mean.
checklist: Names all currently enrolled students as the population.
Identifies the 120 selected students as the sample.
Asks about a mean for the specified population.
